name: title
title: How Far Can Web Architecture Go Toward Zero Tokens?
kicker: Web architecture, measured by Fielding’s own words
html:
How Far Can Web Architecture Go Toward Zero Tokens?

Web architecture, measured by Fielding’s own words. Have you ever paid a model to find the same path twice?

The driver The three R’s The hype

The measuring stick
say: Have you ever paid a model to find the same path twice? Most of us have, this year, many times a day. Kelsey Hightower gave that habit a name and an alternative: Zero Token Architecture. Infer once, then run the result without a model. So here's the question for the next half hour. How far can Web architecture go toward that? Not one person's vision: the architecture the Web already runs on. And we need a measuring stick, so we'll use Roy Fielding's own words: his 2000 dissertation, his 2008 rules, and his complaints about what people did with them. Every colored pill you see is a mark on that stick, and you can click any of them, any time. Tokens are only part of why it matters. The business needs three R's: right behavior, repeatability, and resilience. Reasoning is the part everyone's excited about. We'll keep it at the edges.

deck:ref.name: zta
deck:ref.label: ZTA
deck:ref.title: ZTA: Zero Token Architecture
deck:ref.summary: Agents that run inference on every call burn tokens and work against zero trust. Infer once, then run the result as reliable, deterministic code. (In my words, from the talk's page and Daniel Cranney's write-up.)
deck:ref.quote:
“You are all having way too much fun burning way too many tokens”

His opening line, as quoted in Daniel Cranney, “Infer Once, Run Everywhere: Zero-Token Architecture”, WeAreDevelopers, 13 October 2026.
deck:ref.cite: Kelsey Hightower, WeAreDevelopers World Congress North America

describedby.title: Kelsey Hightower, WeAreDevelopers World Congress North America

deck:ref.name: right-behavior
deck:ref.label: RIGHT-BEHAVIOR
deck:ref.title: Right behavior: only what the state allows, and a reason when not
deck:ref.summary: The agent is offered only the acts the current state allows, sends each one with the validator from the state it read, and gets a reason when an act is absent. At the small scale it is a Gherkin scenario that says what right means before any code is written.
deck:ref.cite: The first of the three R's

describedby.title: The first of the three R's

deck:ref.name: repeatability
deck:ref.label: REPEATABILITY
deck:ref.title: Repeatability: the same goal, the same result, every time
deck:ref.summary: Given the same inputs, the same outputs, call after call. Found once with a model, then replayed with none: the same steps, the same checks, the same result, until the controls really change. At the small scale it is one scenario that runs the same way every time.
deck:ref.cite: The second of the three R's

describedby.title: The second of the three R's

deck:ref.name: resilience
deck:ref.label: RESILIENCE
deck:ref.title: Resilience: the server changes, the client doesn't break
deck:ref.summary: When the server changes, or misbehaves on purpose, the client takes the failure path the spec names, re-syncs, and goes on; a model comes back only when the controls really changed, to repair. At the small scale it is the regression suite and the gates that hold, even against the model.
deck:ref.cite: The third of the three R's

describedby.title: The third of the three R's

deck:ref.name: reason
deck:ref.label: REASON
deck:ref.title: Reason: the part everyone's excited about
deck:ref.summary: Reasoning models can stand in for a person in two places: finding the way the first time, and repairing when the controls change. Everywhere else, paying a model to reason through the same path again is the token maxing Hightower warned about. Useful at the edges; wasted in the middle.

deck:ref.name: uniform-interface
deck:ref.label: UNIFORM-INTERFACE
deck:ref.title: Uniform interface (§5.1.5)
deck:ref.summary: One generic interface for every component; its fourth part is hypermedia as the engine of application state.
deck:ref.quote:
“The central feature that distinguishes the REST architectural style from other network-based styles is its emphasis on a uniform interface between components (Figure 5-6). By applying the software engineering principle of generality to the component interface, the overall system architecture is simplified and the visibility of interactions is improved. Implementations are decoupled from the services they provide, which encourages independent evolvability. The trade-off, though, is that a uniform interface degrades efficiency, since information is transferred in a standardized form rather than one which is specific to an application's needs. The REST interface is designed to be efficient for large-grain hypermedia data transfer, optimizing for the common case of the Web, but resulting in an interface that is not optimal for other forms of architectural interaction.

In order to obtain a uniform interface, multiple architectural constraints are needed to guide the behavior of components. REST is defined by four interface constraints: identification of resources; manipulation of resources through representations; self-descriptive messages; and, hypermedia as the engine of application state. These constraints will be discussed in Section 5.2.”
deck:ref.cite: Roy T. Fielding, Architectural Styles and the Design of Network-based Software Architectures, §5.1.5

describedby.title: Roy T. Fielding, Architectural Styles and the Design of Network-based Software Architectures, §5.1.5

deck:ref.name: rule-6
deck:ref.label: BOOKMARK
deck:ref.title: Enter with a bookmark; follow what's offered
deck:ref.summary: In brief: one URI and known media types to start; every next step chosen from what the server put in the answer.
deck:ref.quote: “A REST API should be entered with no prior knowledge beyond the initial URI (bookmark) and set of standardized media types that are appropriate for the intended audience (i.e., expected to be understood by any client that might use the API). From that point on, all application state transitions must be driven by client selection of server-provided choices that are present in the received representations or implied by the user’s manipulation of those representations. The transitions may be determined (or limited by) the client’s knowledge of media types and resource communication mechanisms, both of which may be improved on-the-fly (e.g., code-on-demand). [Failure here implies that out-of-band information is driving interaction instead of hypertext.]”
deck:ref.cite: Roy T. Fielding, “REST APIs must be hypertext-driven”

describedby.title: Roy T. Fielding, “REST APIs must be hypertext-driven”

deck:ref.name: hypertext
deck:ref.label: HYPERTEXT
deck:ref.title: What hypertext means
deck:ref.summary: His definition: information and controls, presented together. Machines can follow links too.
deck:ref.quote:
“When I say hypertext, I mean the simultaneous presentation of information and controls such that the information becomes the affordance through which the user (or automaton) obtains choices and selects actions. Hypermedia is just an expansion on what text means to include temporal anchors within a media stream; most researchers have dropped the distinction.

Hypertext does not need to be HTML on a browser. Machines can follow links when they understand the data format and relationship types.”
deck:ref.cite: Roy T. Fielding, comment on “REST APIs must be hypertext-driven”

describedby.title: Roy T. Fielding, comment on “REST APIs must be hypertext-driven”

deck:ref.name: frustrated
deck:ref.label: FRUSTRATED
deck:ref.title: “I am getting frustrated…”
deck:ref.summary: Why he wrote the six rules.
deck:ref.quote:
“I am getting frustrated by the number of people calling any HTTP-based interface a REST API. Today’s example is the SocialSite REST API. That is RPC. It screams RPC. There is so much coupling on display that it should be given an X rating.

What needs to be done to make the REST architectural style clear on the notion that hypertext is a constraint? In other words, if the engine of application state (and hence the API) is not being driven by hypertext, then it cannot be RESTful and cannot be a REST API. Period. Is there some broken manual somewhere that needs to be fixed?”
deck:ref.cite: Roy T. Fielding, “REST APIs must be hypertext-driven”

describedby.title: Roy T. Fielding, “REST APIs must be hypertext-driven”
